questions.prompt: Two branches lead out of one node. Both end with the same line three nodes later. What's the problem?

options.label: If both branches land in the same place, the choice didn't really branch — the reader feels the trick.
No problem. Reaching the same line means the dialogue tree is balanced.
The branches should be longer so the reader forgets they merged.

questions.mentorPostScript: Sprig says: a branch should re-route the story so the reader can feel it.

questions.prompt: Iris just said something cruel. Cal has two branches: "Apologize" or "Walk away." Which detail makes the branches feel like real choices?

options.label: Each branch costs Cal something different — apologizing means swallowing pride; walking away means losing the friendship that night.
Both branches lead to a new scene the next day.
Both branches end with Cal smiling.

questions.mentorPostScript: When each side costs the speaker something different, the choice matters.

questions.prompt: A branch point asks the kid to pick what the character SAYS next. Where should the consequence land?

options.label: On the OTHER character — what they say back changes based on what was just said.
Nowhere — branches are just for variety.
On the speaker — they should always agree with their own choice.

questions.mentorPostScript: Real branches change how the next speaker responds. That's the re-route the reader feels.

questions.prompt: Mara is choosing between confessing to Cal or staying quiet. Which version of the branch is most meaningful?

options.label: Confess → Cal's tone shifts for the rest of the scene; Stay quiet → Cal stays warm but Mara loses something inside.
Confess → the next line is a joke; Stay quiet → the next line is also a joke.
Confess → the scene ends; Stay quiet → the scene also ends.

questions.mentorPostScript: Either path should leave a mark the reader can name.

questions.prompt: You're writing a branch where one side is the "safe" choice and the other is risky. The risky side should:

options.label: Actually risk something — a friendship, a secret, a chance — so the reader feels the speaker's heart in their throat.
Be the same as the safe choice but with bigger words.
Always lead to a happy ending so the reader doesn't worry.

questions.mentorPostScript: If a risky choice doesn't risk anything, the reader smells the pretend.
